stem:
An emergency doctor assesses a 17-year-old who has severely restricted her eating and lost 18% of her body weight over three months. Her BMI is now 21 kg/m², and her parents point out that she is “not even underweight”. She has fainted twice this week. Her awake heart rate is 38/min and she becomes dizzy on standing. She is not an endurance athlete and has no current suicidal intent.

What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.label: A
options.text: Discharge with dietitian follow-up, as her BMI is normal
options.explanation: A normal BMI does not exclude medical instability; rapid weight loss is the danger here.

options.label: B
options.text: An urgent outpatient eating-disorder clinic appointment
options.explanation: Specialist outpatient care is appropriate once she is medically stable. Bradycardia of 38/min with syncope needs inpatient monitoring now.

options.label: C
options.text: Transfer to the mental health unit for supervised meals
options.explanation: A mental health unit usually cannot provide the cardiac monitoring and refeeding care that her bradycardia and syncope require.

options.label: D
options.text: Medical ward admission with specialist team input
options.explanation: Marked bradycardia, syncope and postural symptoms after rapid weight loss indicate medical instability. She needs admission to a medical (adolescent) ward for monitoring and supervised refeeding, with eating-disorder team involvement.

options.label: E
options.text: Weekly weighing by her GP while awaiting psychotherapy
options.explanation: Weekly GP review leaves an unstable adolescent without monitoring and delays treatment.

context: Rapid weight loss can cause dangerous medical instability at a normal-range BMI; bradycardia, syncope and postural symptoms decide admission, not the BMI.
